messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: ESS confusion
parts:
Hi!

Sorry for this naive question, but I run a standard hierarchical model, get regression coefficient and between-trial heterogeneity parameters tau which I use to make a prediction. For follow up analyses (of the prediction) I thin down the sample to it's effective sample size. The thinning is done with repsect to the ESS, but which one should I take:

R3.0.2> gbin_stan$ESS
$beta
[1] 946.6441

$tau
[1] 101.3539

$lp
[1] 58.31506

$theta_resp.pred
[1] 2774.734


Should I use a geometric mean, the minimum or the ESS from theta_resp.pred which is what I use in my follow-up?

Thanks.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ESS confusion
parts:
Effective sample size is defined with respect to
a parameter, so asking for the effective sample
size of the entire chain is ill-posed.

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: ESS confusion
parts: For follow up analyses (of the prediction) I thin down the sample to it's effective sample size.

In addition to others comments, even if you are examining one quantity, note that if you were going to select ESS number of draws from the whole sample, then the effective sample size for the thinned set is likely to be smaller than the original ESS as the thinning throws away information. If you want to thin to get almost independent draws to simplify the follow up analysis, you need to look at the autocorrelations and not ESS.

Aki

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: ESS confusion
parts:
Hi all,

thanks a lot. I guess I have to look at the definitions to see what makes most sense in my application. What Aki points out seems to be closest to what I am looking for, i.e. a sample which has no autocorrelations. I thought this is about what ESS would tell me (but the naming here may be misleading).

BTW, throwing away a bit of information is not an issue - Stan is so efficient and generates huge ESS in no time for my problem, I rather have a memory and speed problem in follow up analyses if I were to keep all samples.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ESS confusion
parts:
No, the name's not misleading. The ESS is an estimate of the
statistical power of the sample you have scaled to the number of
i.i.d. draws to which it would be equivalent.

What happens is that a sequence of autocorrelated draws have more
power than thinning because there's information in the thinned draws
that gets lost when you thin them.

There's a very nice overview in Geyer's chapter for the MCMC
Handbook, which is one of the free samples:

http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf

Just don't listen to his advice on convergence monitoring! His
comments are right in theory, but not in practice if you want
answers in finite amounts of time.

And we do our calculations a little differently, as described in
BDA3 and in the manual --- we basically take cross-chain information
into account, which makes our ESS calculations more conservative than
the typical approach of estimating each chain separately (they give
you the same answer in the stationary limit).

- Bob

parts:
I can see why "power" is bad, but why "information"?
I tend to think of information content as being measured
by things like entropy. Is it by analogy to the expected
information about the mean contained in N i.i.d. draws?

I never quantify any units or other generic nouns in the manual.

Geyer uses "statistical accuracy", in the context "statistical accuracy
is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size",
which also seems sub-optimal terminologically.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ESS confusion
parts:
- Information is already used as a property of a distribution
- Thinning _always_ removes information unless your chain is perfectly autocorrelated
- Remember that all of this conversation is still based on the fact
that all of these measures depend on a function whose expectation
you are taking. So there is no single “statistical accuracy” or “effective
sample size” for the entire chain in isolation, just for a single chain with
respect to a given function.

>>>> BTW, throwing away a bit of information is not an issue - Stan is so efficient and generates huge ESS in no time for my problem, I rather have a memory and speed problem in follow up analyses if I were to keep all samples.
>>>>
>>>> On Friday, July 31, 2015 at 10:50:06 PM UTC+2, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>>>>
>>>> For follow up analyses (of the prediction) I thin down the sample to it's effective sample size.
>>>>
>>>> In addition to others comments, even if you are examining one quantity, note that if you were going to select ESS number of draws from the whole sample, then the effective sample size for the thinned set is likely to be smaller than the original ESS as the thinning throws away information. If you want to thin to get almost independent draws to simplify the follow up analysis, you need to look at the autocorrelations and not ESS.
>>>>
>>>> Aki

On Sunday, August 2, 2015 at 6:01:29 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Hi, yes, information is sometimes defined as inverse variance, so it’s pretty close to what we’re talking about here.  “Power” would be fine except that that term is already taken.
How about precision instead of information?
